passages.where: After Carmel and the threat that followed, Elijah lies down under a broom tree and sleeps, and an angel wakes him twice to eat, saying the way ahead will be too much for him. The site's note names exhaustion after great effort and fear of a real threat in the text, and says God's response is striking in its order: rest, food, water and a second meal before any words. The note adds that the chapter treats such feelings as real without treating them as the final word.

Traveling through Samaria, Jesus is tired from the road and sits down by Jacob's well at the sixth hour. The site's plain note says he is not too holy to be weary. The Son of God took on tiredness with the rest of our humanity.

To exiles who say their way is hidden from God, Isaiah answers that the everlasting God does not grow tired and that he gives power to the faint. The site's note says even the fittest young men tire and stumble, but those who wait for the LORD exchange their strength for his. The promise is spoken to the faint, not to people who have stopped being tired.

Moses, overwhelmed by the people's complaints, has told God he cannot carry them all by himself, and God has him gather seventy elders to share the Spirit and the burden. The site's note says the seventy were already recognized leaders, whom God equips for a shared burden. God's answer to a leader at the end of his strength is other people, so that he does not have to bear it by himself.

David, weak in body and shaken in soul, says he is weary from groaning and floods his bed with tears all night. The site's plain note says the tears were not a failure of faith and that lament is not unbelief. It also says that anyone whose nights are like these should not carry them alone.

Paul, pressed and perplexed in his work, says that though the outer self is wasting away, the inner self is being renewed day by day. The site's note says he does not pretend that faith makes people immune to despair. The chapter's not crushed is not a demand that believers feel strong, but a testimony that God held Paul when he could not hold himself.

The shepherd makes his sheep lie down in green pastures, leads them beside quiet waters and restores the soul. The site's plain note says to read the psalm as a sheep, which survives because someone looks after it, and that the psalm asks you to admit that you need looking after. Rest here is something the shepherd gives, and even makes his sheep take.

The psalm says it is in vain to rise early and stay up late toiling for bread, for the LORD gives sleep to his beloved. The site's plain note says it does not tell anyone to stop working, but that worry is not the same as work. Lying down to rest, it says, can be an act of trust: God keeps the city while you sleep.

When the apostles come back and report all they have done and taught, Jesus invites them to a solitary place to rest, because so many people were coming and going that they did not even have time to eat. The site's note sets the invitation right after their report. Jesus noticed that the people working with him had not eaten.

The book's closing voice warns that there is no end to the making of many books, and that much study wearies the body. The site's note calls this voice the frame narrator, who gives the book's conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments. The Bible itself names a limit to what the mind can take in.

misread.taken: Come to Me and My yoke is easy are heard by worn-out people as one more demand: if you are still tired, you must not be trusting Jesus enough, so pray more, try harder and do better.
misread.says: The site's plain note says many people have heard this invitation as one more demand, try harder, pray more, do better, and that it is not a demand but an invitation from a person: come to me. Jesus is not promising that there will be no load; he promises that his load fits and that you do not carry it alone, for a yoke is made for two. The note says that anyone worn out, by grief, by guilt, by caring for someone or by a religion that felt like a weight, is the one these words are spoken to.

whole: If exhaustion has come with despair, with thoughts of hurting yourself, or with weeks of lost sleep and appetite, tell someone you trust today, a doctor, a pastor or a friend, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Exhaustion of this kind can be part of depression or of an illness in the body, and seeing a doctor about it is not a failure of faith. Mental exhaustion is different from being tired after a long day. People describe a mind that will not hold a thought, a short temper over small things, reading the same paragraph three times, dreading the next message, waking already tired. Sleep helps less than it should. Those who feel it often believe they have no right to stop.

Scripture does not treat this as a weakness of character. Jesus himself was tired from the road and sat down at a well. Moses was overwhelmed by the weight of the people and told God he could not carry them by himself. David was weary from groaning, and Elijah, after the strain of Carmel and the threat that followed it, lay down under a tree and slept. Part of what wears a mind down is real load: too many people depending on one person, too little sleep, grief, illness, no day that is not given to someone else. Part of it is a belief beneath the load, that everything depends on us and that stopping would mean failing God or the people we love. Psalm 127 calls that rising early and staying up late in vain, and many of us live by it without ever saying it aloud.

So the Bible's wisdom begins with the body. God answered Elijah with sleep, bread and water before he said anything about the work, and Jesus took his disciples away to rest when they had not had time to eat. It goes on to other people: God gave Moses seventy elders so that he would not bear the burden by himself, and it is wise to ask who could carry part of yours. It names limits for the mind as well as the hands; the closing voice of Ecclesiastes says much study wearies the body. And it treats rest as trust rather than laziness. The LORD gives sleep to his beloved, and lying down can be a way of saying that he keeps the city and you do not have to. If the tiredness lasts for weeks, or comes with sadness, a doctor should hear about it.

The hope Scripture gives is a God who does not grow tired and who gives power to the faint. Paul's outer self was wasting away, and he said his inner self was being renewed day by day, not all at once. The shepherd makes his sheep lie down, and Jesus invites the worn out to come to him, not to fix themselves first, and offers a yoke that is made for two. You are not asked to be endless. You are invited to be carried, and to rest while someone else keeps watch.
sit: What is one load you are carrying as if everything depended on you, and who could carry part of it with you this week?

prayer.lead: A prayer for when the heart is faint. The site's plain note says that when your heart is faint you cannot lift yourself, and you need something firmer than you are, and someone to lead you to it.

careLines.text: If you are in a dark place now, you do not have to pretend to be strong, and you do not have to carry it alone.
Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor, or a friend.
When grief or sadness lasts and starts taking sleep, appetite or work, seeing a doctor is wise, and it is not a failure of faith.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
